why: The web server handles everything in one process on one event loop. A slow image provider, a heavy photo decode, a database call or a retry storm could freeze every customer's messages, strand paid orders, or burn the daily spending limit on failed calls. The audit predicted these failures under a burst of 100 requests a minute. Without this phase one slow minute at one provider could make the whole bot unresponsive and customers could pay for orders that never complete.
approach: Slow or heavy work moved off the main loop into separate worker pools; database connections are given back before any long wait; every outside call has a deadline and a sensible retry rule; a shared daily counter in the database caps AI spending across all processes and gives slots back when a call fails; and a repeatable load test with eleven scenarios proves each fix.

decisions.decision: Use separate worker pools for CPU work (photo decoding), database/file work and network sends, sized from the machine's cores.
decisions.why: One shared pool let slow network calls starve photo decoding and vice versa. Separate pools keep each kind of work from blocking the others, and the load test showed the longest loop stall dropping from 2.7 seconds to under 0.1 second.

alternatives.why_not: Unbounded mixing of work types; measured stalls up to 2.7 seconds.
Much more memory and complexity for the same benefit at this size.

decisions.decision: Count the daily AI ceiling in a database table shared by every server process, with a guarded update, and give slots back when a call fails.
decisions.why: An in-memory counter is per process (two processes = double the ceiling) and was never given back after failures, so failed orders ate the limit.

alternatives.why_not: Needs a new service the owner has not chosen yet; the database already exists.

alternatives.option: Per-process counter divided by process count
alternatives.why_not: Wrong whenever processes restart or differ in load.

decisions.decision: Separate a per-minute rate limit (retry, then fall back) from billing or daily-quota exhaustion (halt, refund, do not fall back).
decisions.why: The same Gemini wording appears for both. Treating a short rate limit as 'out of money' made orders fail needlessly; treating a real quota exhaustion as retryable burned the second provider's money.

alternatives.why_not: Would hammer a provider with an exhausted account.
Failed orders that a ten-second wait would have served.

decisions.decision: Bound only the GENERATION part of a Catalog Pack with a deadline; a style that finished in time is always uploaded and delivered.
decisions.why: A deadline over the whole job could cut a finished image off in the middle of its upload, wasting a paid call.

alternatives.option: One deadline for generation plus upload

errors.error: TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out
errors.cause: A product-choice handler held a database connection while it waited on another thread that needed its own, so bursts of 16 or more orders ran out of connections.
errors.fix: End the transaction before the wait. Load scenario k now proves 30 simultaneous orders complete.

errors.error: AttributeError: 'Depends' object has no attribute 'append' (load harness)
errors.cause: The harness called the webhook function directly, so the tracking dependency was a placeholder object.
errors.fix: The webhook tolerates being called without the dependency (duplicate protection still works). A test-harness workaround.

errors.error: Reviewer: refund could be skipped when a 5xx came after the provider had accepted a send
errors.cause: Message sends were retried on 5xx; a retry after a half-delivered send could duplicate it.
errors.fix: Sends retry only on 429 and connection failures, never on 5xx.
